title: S-Corp Reasonable Compensation: Setting the Owner’s Salary Defensibly
summary: S-corp reasonable compensation has no IRS safe harbor. See the nine-factor test, the 2026 payroll figures, and how to document an owner salary that holds.
body_markdown:
## What Reasonable Compensation Triggers


S-corp reasonable compensation is the W-2 wage an S corporation owes a shareholder who performs more than minor services, before it pays any non-wage distribution.


The trigger is services, not revenue.


Treasury’s regulation at 26 CFR 31.3121(d)-1(b) is the cleanest statement of the rule. An officer of a corporation is an employee. The only exception covers an officer who performs no services or only minor services **and** who neither receives nor is entitled to receive any remuneration. Note the conjunction. Both halves have to be true.


A founder who runs the company and takes $0 in wages fails that exception, because the services are real. A passive shareholder who shows up for one annual board vote and draws nothing meets it. The IRS states the affirmative side on its page covering[S corporation employees, shareholders and corporate officers](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/s-corporation-employees-shareholders-and-corporate-officers) , and the same page closes the obvious workaround. Shareholder-employees are subject to employment taxes even when they take distributions, dividends, or other forms of compensation instead of wages.


The obligation attaches in the first year the company has earnings available to distribute and the shareholder performs services. No grace period, no first-year exemption, no revenue floor.


Three consequences of framing the trigger around services rather than profit:


- **A pre-revenue company and a pre-profit company carry different risk.** Reclassification runs against payments made, not profit earned. A company with no cash to distribute has less to reclassify. A company moving cash to the owner has a target from day one.
- **A loss year doesn’t suspend the rule.** In Glass Blocks Unlimited v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2013-180, the corporation reported losses and the sole shareholder called his withdrawals loan repayments. The Tax Court held the earlier transfers in were capital contributions rather than bona fide loans, so the withdrawals out were wages.
- **Routing the owner through a 1099 doesn’t work either.** In Joseph M. Grey Public Accountant, P.C. v. Commissioner, 119 T.C. 121 (2002), the sole shareholder took the entire taxable income as independent contractor fees. The court held he was an employee and recharacterized the fees as wages. The question of whether[an S corp gets a 1099](https://www.indinero.com/faq/does-an-s-corp-get-1099/) has a different answer than the question of how its owner gets paid.


The scale of the problem is documented. The Government Accountability Office’s 2009 study of S corporation noncompliance put net shareholder compensation underreporting at roughly $23.6 billion across the 2003 and 2004 tax years, found that about 68 percent of S corporation returns for those years misreported at least one item, and found that misreporting favored the corporation or the shareholder about 80 percent of the time. The same report told IRS examiners to document their analysis using comparable salary data.


This page assumes the election is already made. If you’re still choosing, our comparison of[a C corp and an S corp](https://www.indinero.com/blog/c-corp-vs-s-corp/) and the walkthrough of[the Form 2553 election](https://www.indinero.com/blog/irs-form-2553/) cover that decision instead.


## Federal Requirements


Shareholder-employee wages run through payroll like any other employee’s, because IRC 3121(d)(1) defines employee to include any officer of a corporation.


That’s a statutory inclusion, not a facts-and-circumstances test. The worker-classification arguments that reach contractors don’t reach an S-corp officer.


The reclassification power isn’t new either. Rev. Rul. 74-44 held that distributions arranged in lieu of salary are wages, imputed reasonable salaries, and held the corporation liable for FICA, FUTA, and income tax withholding on those amounts. S-corp distributions reclassified as wages carry the employment tax plus penalties and interest, and the IRS restates that authority plainly on its page covering[S corporation compensation and medical insurance issues](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/s-corporation-compensation-and-medical-insurance-issues) .


### Officers are statutory employees


An S-corp owner salary carries the same federal machinery as any other paycheck. Social Security and Medicare withholding, federal income tax withholding, a quarterly Form 941, an annual Form 940 for FUTA, and a Form W-2 at year end. There is no reduced-compliance version of owner payroll, and no filing that exists to report an owner’s wage in some other way.


That matters because the officer rule sits in the statute rather than in a test. A company can argue about whether a developer in another state is a contractor. It cannot argue that a working officer is outside the definition of employee. If you’re sorting out the basics of[how an S corp is taxed](https://www.indinero.com/faq/what-is-an-s-corp/) , start there, because the payroll obligation follows from the structure, not from a choice.


### The 2026 figures that set the cost


Item 2026 figure


Social Security (OASDI) wage base $184,500


OASDI rate, employer and employee each 6.2 percent


Medicare rate, employer and employee each 1.45 percent


Combined FICA up to the wage base 15.3 percent


Additional Medicare Tax 0.9 percent on wages over $200,000, employee only, no employer match


Maximum employee OASDI contribution $11,439.00


FUTA 6.0 percent on the first $7,000, net 0.6 percent after the 5.4 percent credit


The wage base and the maximum employee contribution come from the Social Security Administration’s[contribution and benefit base](https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html) table, and the rates sit in IRS Topic no. 751.


Read the shape of that table, not just the numbers. Every dollar of owner wage below $184,500 costs 15.3 percent across both halves. Above the wage base the marginal cost is Medicare only, 2.9 percent across both halves, rising by the employee’s 0.9 percent once wages pass $200,000. The entire financial argument for a low owner salary lives inside that first $184,500, which is also the range where the other three effects on this page are largest.


### How examiners frame the question


The IRS starts with the source of the company’s gross receipts, not with the owner’s title. Its compensation page names three sources: services of the shareholder, services of non-shareholder employees, and capital and equipment. The share of receipts traceable to the shareholder’s own services is the share that has to be paid as wages.


That split is the argument. A software company whose revenue comes from a product built by twelve engineers and sold by a sales team has a real case that receipts flow from non-shareholder services and from capital. A one-person consultancy billing the founder’s hours does not.


From there, nine factors govern, drawn from the IRS compensation page and Fact Sheet FS-2008-25:


- Training and experience
- Duties and responsibilities
- Time and effort devoted to the business
- Dividend history
- Payments to non-shareholder employees
- Timing and manner of paying bonuses to key people
- What comparable businesses pay for similar services
- Compensation agreements
- The use of a formula to determine compensation


### No safe harbor, no percentage, no formula


Searches for a reasonable salary for S-corp owner pay are looking for a published figure. There isn’t one.


No Code section, no regulation, no revenue ruling, and no reported case establishes a 60/40 split, a one-third rule, a 50/50 rule, or any other ratio as reasonable compensation. The ninth factor above cuts the other way. The IRS treats the use of a formula as one fact among nine, which makes a formula evidence about your process rather than a defense of your number.


The absence of a bright line is a documented policy problem, not an oversight. GAO found the standard highly subjective and said the IRS provides limited guidance on determining adequate compensation. Treat percentage rules of thumb the way you’d treat any other number nobody will stand behind in writing.


### What the courts actually awarded


Three cases carry the useful numbers.


- **David E. Watson, P.C. v. United States, 668 F.3d 1008 (8th Cir. 2012).** Watson’s professional corporation paid him $24,000 a year while distributing $203,651 in 2002 and $175,470 in 2003. The government’s expert built a figure from the AICPA Management of an Accounting Practice survey and other wage data, landing at $91,044 after adjusting for non-taxable fringe benefits. The district court adopted it for both years, reclassifying $67,044 of distributions annually, and the Eighth Circuit affirmed.
- **JD & Associates, Ltd. v. United States, D.N.D. docket 3:04-cv-00059.** The sole shareholder of a Fargo accounting firm drew $19,000 in 1997 and $30,000 in each of 1998 and 1999. The IRS expert used Risk Management Association ratios to show the firm was 200 to 300 percent more profitable than peers while the owner’s pay sat 166 to 266 percent below peer CPAs. The court set compensation at $69,584, $79,823, and $79,711, sustaining reclassification of $42,817, $33,072, and $35,582.
- **Sean McAlary Ltd., Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Summ. 2013-62.** The corporation issued no Form W-2 and claimed no wage deduction while the owner moved $240,000 out of the corporate account. The IRS valuation expert said $100,755. The court settled on $83,200, built from a $40 per hour rate, and refused to be bound by a written agreement setting base pay at $24,000 because it wasn’t arm’s-length and wasn’t followed in practice.


Two readings matter. Watson still kept more than $110,000 in 2002 and roughly $85,000 in 2003 as distributions, so reasonable compensation is a market wage, not all the profit. And in McAlary, the paperwork didn’t save the number. An agreement only helps if the company actually pays it.


### Where the number lands on the return


Form 1120-S reports officer compensation on line 7, separately from line 8 for other salaries and wages. A return showing material profit with $0 on line 7 is a visible anomaly, and it is visible before anyone opens an exam.


Form 1125-E raises the disclosure. The instructions require it whenever the entity has total receipts of $500,000 or more and deducts compensation for officers, and line 1 captures salaries, commissions, bonuses, and taxable fringe benefits. At that point the return names the officer, the percentage of stock owned, the percentage of time devoted to the business, and the compensation amount, all on one schedule. Growth makes a stale owner salary sharper, not softer, because the percentage of time column sits two inches from the dollar figure.


### Three ways to build the number


Regs. Sec. 1.162-7(b)(3) sets the standard: the value that would ordinarily be paid for like services by like enterprises under like circumstances. Practitioners get there three ways.


- **Cost approach, sometimes called many hats.** Decompose the owner’s duties into discrete roles, price each against wage survey data, and weight by hours. Best fit for an owner-operator wearing four hats at fifteen hours each.
- **Market approach.** Compare the owner against non-owner pay for the same position in the same industry and geography. Best fit where a true comparable exists, which is what the government built in Watson.
- **Income approach, the independent-investor test.** Ask whether an outside investor would accept the return left after compensation. Mulcahy, Pauritsch, Salvador & Co., Ltd. v. Commissioner, 680 F.3d 867 (7th Cir. 2012) applied that framework where comparability data was thin.


For the underlying data, use the Bureau of Labor Statistics[Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/oes/) program, which publishes annual employment and wage estimates for roughly 830 occupations at national, state, and metropolitan level, with a May 2025 reference period. OEWS gives you an SOC code, a geography, and a wage distribution. That is the shape of evidence GAO told examiners to look for, and it’s free. Salary-by-industry tables published by software vendors are not survey data and don’t carry the same weight in a file.


### The Section 199A interaction runs in two directions


This is where most competing pages stop, and they stop halfway.


Owner wages are not QBI. The IRS qualified business income guidance excludes amounts received as reasonable compensation from an S corporation, so every dollar moved from distribution to salary leaves the 20 percent base. That’s the effect everyone knows.


Owner wages also feed the limitation. Under IRC 199A(b)(2), the per-business deduction is capped at the greater of 50 percent of W-2 wages paid by the business, or 25 percent of W-2 wages plus 2.5 percent of the unadjusted basis of qualified property. For an asset-light service or software company with little qualified property, the 50 percent of wages test is the operative cap, and a low owner salary at a company with few other employees can cut the deduction to a fraction of 20 percent of QBI.


Which effect wins depends on taxable income against the 2026 figures in Rev. Proc. 2025-32, published in[Internal Revenue Bulletin 2025-45](https://www.irs.gov/irb/2025-45_IRB) :


Filing status Threshold amount Phase-in range amount


Married filing jointly $403,500 $553,500


All other returns $201,750 $276,750


Below the threshold the wage limitation doesn’t apply at all, so a low salary maximizes the deduction and the 199A effect runs against paying more. Above the top of the phase-in range the limitation applies in full, so a low salary can gut the deduction. Inside the band it’s a blend. The same revenue procedure carries the OBBBA addition of a minimum $400 deduction for taxpayers with at least $1,000 of qualified business income, for years beginning after December 31, 2025.


One more limit, and it’s a hard one. For a specified service trade or business above the top of the phase-in range, the 199A deduction is zero whatever the salary, so the offset described here doesn’t exist. Run it, don’t assume it.


### Retirement capacity and the more-than-2-percent shareholder premium


Every qualified plan limit sits on W-2 compensation, so too low a salary caps the plan. The 2026 figures from the IRS cost-of-living adjustment tables are a $24,500 elective deferral under 402(g), $8,000 of catch-up at age 50 and over, $72,000 of annual additions under 415(c), and a $360,000 compensation limit under 401(a)(17). The employer side is the binding constraint, because IRC 404(a)(3)(A)(i) caps the profit-sharing deduction at 25 percent of compensation paid.


Run it. Reaching the full $72,000 through a solo 401(k) with a 25 percent employer contribution plus the deferral takes about $190,000 of W-2 compensation. At a $60,000 salary the ceiling is $39,500. The low salary costs $32,500 of deductible retirement capacity before any other effect is counted.


Health premiums move the other way. For a greater-than-2-percent shareholder-employee, premiums are deductible by the corporation and reportable as wages on the W-2 subject to income tax withholding, but not subject to Social Security, Medicare, or FUTA. Box 1 yes, Boxes 3 and 5 no. Notice 2008-1 then requires the corporation to report those premiums as wages on the W-2 in the same year, or the shareholder loses the Section 162(l) deduction entirely. Because the add-on is FICA-exempt, it raises reported W-2 compensation without raising payroll tax, which is also the adjustment the Watson expert made in moving from $93,000 to $91,044.


## State Requirements


Owner wages are sourced to the state where the work is performed, not the state of incorporation, and several states then tax the wage and the distribution differently.


### Withholding follows the work


A Delaware-incorporated S corp with a founder working from Denver has a Colorado withholding registration obligation on the owner’s own paycheck. Nine states impose no broad individual income tax on wages, which removes the withholding question there but not the unemployment or workers’ comp questions below.


For a company with employees in four states, the owner’s paycheck is one row in a much larger registration problem. The sequence, the account numbers, and the per-state filing cadence are the same ones covered in our guide to[multi-state payroll compliance for growing SaaS](https://www.indinero.com/blog/multi-state-payroll-compliance-for-growing-saas/) . The difference with owner wages is that nobody from recruiting flags them, because the owner was never a new hire.


### Unemployment and workers’ comp flip by state


This is the most commonly missed state item, because the default itself changes by state.


Washington excludes corporate officers from unemployment insurance by default. Its[Employment Security Department](https://esd.wa.gov/employer-requirements/quarterly-reports/unemployment-coverage-corporate-officers) treats officers of for-profit corporations who provide services in the state as exempt unless the employer specifically requests coverage, which means filing a voluntary election form and submitting it by the chosen quarter’s due date. Elected coverage has to run at least two full calendar years, and ending it takes a written request by January 15. An officer owning 10 percent or more of the stock may then be ineligible for benefits anyway unless narrow conditions apply. In Washington the default is no coverage and no benefit, and paying the tax voluntarily can buy a benefit the ownership rule denies.


California splits the two. Under Section 637.1 of the Unemployment Insurance Code, a corporate officer who is the sole shareholder, or the only shareholder other than a spouse, can file Form DE 459 to be excluded from State Disability Insurance only, including Paid Family Leave. The corporation still reports wages and pays Unemployment Insurance and Employment Training Tax. The exclusion takes effect the first day of the quarter in which it’s filed and then locks in for the rest of that year plus at least two more.


Workers’ comp runs on its own elections. California requires executive officers and directors to be covered unless the corporation is fully owned by its directors and officers, in which case they may elect out. Washington exempts an officer only if three conditions all hold, including stock issued in their name and substantial control in daily management. Texas allows exclusion of an executive officer with at least 25 percent equity by attaching the right endorsement.


It’s a calendar item, not a return item.


### California: three taxes moving in different directions


California taxes an S corporation with California source income at 1.5 percent, with an $800 annual minimum franchise tax, and the liability is the greater of the two. The minimum is waived for a newly formed corporation’s first taxable year. These figures are the Franchise Tax Board’s, and the return is Form 100S.


Because owner wages are deductible in computing California net income, raising the owner’s salary reduces the 1.5 percent entity tax. A $100,000 salary increase cuts it by $1,500. Small, and it moves opposite the federal FICA cost, which is why almost nobody models it.


The pass-through entity elective tax pulls the other way. The FTB’s analysis of Senate Bill 132 extends the PTE elective tax for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2026 and before January 1, 2031, at 9.3 percent of each consenting owner’s share of income subject to California personal income tax. That base is distributive income, computed after the wage deduction. Every dollar shifted from distribution to salary leaves the PTE base and loses the federal benefit of the entity-level deduction that Notice 2020-75 permits. With the SALT limitation now permanent and the 2026 cap set at $40,400, reduced above $505,000 of modified adjusted gross income but never below $10,000, the PTE election still matters for most owner-operators, and the wage split still moves it.


### New York City, Tennessee, and New Hampshire move the other way


New York City doesn’t recognize the federal or New York State S election. A federal S corporation doing business, employing capital, owning property, or maintaining an office in the city falls under the[General Corporation Tax](https://www.nyc.gov/site/finance/business/business-general-corporation-tax-gct.page) , which computes tax on the highest of several bases. One of those bases adds back compensation paid to any person owning more than 5 percent of the stock, including an officer. Secondary sources put that alternative base at 8.85 percent of the sum of 15 percent of net income plus that compensation. The qualitative point is the one that changes decisions. In New York City, raising the owner’s salary doesn’t reduce the alternative base, because the salary goes straight back in.


New York State needs its own election. Without Form CT-6, a federal S corporation pays the same corporate franchise taxes as a C corporation, credits stay at the entity level, and resident shareholders are taxed on actual distributions rather than pass-through items.


Tennessee runs the opposite computation. Its 6.5 percent excise tax applies to net earnings determined as if the corporation had never elected S status, so the owner’s salary is deductible and a higher salary reduces the Tennessee tax by 6.5 cents on the dollar.


New Hampshire taxes the compensation itself. The Business Enterprise Tax applies at 0.55 percent to an enterprise value tax base defined as compensation, interest, and dividends paid, with the filing threshold at $250,000 through the end of 2026 and $400,000 from January 1, 2027. So a higher owner salary deducts against the Business Profits Tax base while increasing the BET base. Two moving bases, not one. Other states depart from federal S treatment in their own ways, which is why a multi-state owner needs the state list actually run rather than a national rule of thumb.


## Common Mistakes


Most reasonable-compensation failures aren’t aggressive positions. They’re a number set once, never revisited, and never documented.


1.


**Running no payroll at all.** The most common and the most expensive. No Form 941, no W-2, and 100 percent of owner cash taken as distributions. Glass Blocks Unlimited and Sean McAlary are both exactly this pattern, and both lost. The cost is the employment tax plus failure-to-deposit penalties of up to 15 percent under IRC 6656, information return penalties of $340 each under Sections 6721 and 6722 for a missing W-2 due in 2027, interest, and personal liability for 100 percent of the trust-fund portion under IRC 6672. There’s a quieter loss too. No W-2 means no W-2 wages for Section 199A, so the wage-and-capital limitation can cut the deduction to the qualified-property amount, which for an asset-light company is close to zero.


2.


**The December catch-up payroll run.** Four problems arrive together. A single large payroll can trip the $100,000 next-day deposit rule, which then forces semiweekly depositor status for the rest of the year and all of the next one, as[IRS Topic no. 757](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc757) lays out. Section 199A(b)(4)(C) excludes W-2 wages from the wage limitation unless the amount is properly included in a return filed with the Social Security Administration by the 60th day after its due date, with the computation methods in Rev. Proc. 2019-11, so a scramble that produces a late or corrected W-2 can forfeit the limitation on a technicality. Midwest Eye Center v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2015-53 rejected after-the-fact estimates and put the burden on the shareholder to prove the services provided. And one December run compresses a year of withholding into one period. The fix is boring. A monthly or semimonthly owner payroll, which is how indinero runs owner compensation, keeps the deposits inside the normal schedule and gets the W-2 filed well inside the 60-day window.


3.


**Anchoring on 60/40, one-third, or any other ratio.** There’s no authority behind any of them. The IRS lists the use of a formula as one of nine factors, so a ratio describes your process without defending your number. McAlary is the direct rebuttal, where the court refused to be bound by a written agreement because the figure wasn’t arm’s-length and wasn’t followed.


4.


**Flat salary while profit triples.** Dividend history and payments to non-shareholder employees are two of the nine factors. A static $48,000 officer salary against distributions climbing from $40,000 to $400,000 over four years is the JD & Associates pattern, where the expert showed a firm far more profitable than peers paying an owner far below them. Once total receipts hit $500,000, Form 1125-E also asks for the officer’s percentage of time devoted to the business right next to the compensation figure.


5.


**Documenting nothing.** Substantiating compensatory intent takes board minutes, records of duties and hours, issued Forms W-2, paid employment taxes, filed payroll returns, and financial statements that agree with all of it. The minimum defensible file is an OEWS comparability printout with the SOC code and geography, a written compensation agreement signed before the year begins, board minutes recording the determination and the data relied on, and time records tying hours to roles. Auditors also look for contradicting evidence on your website and in your own marketing, so the role description in the file should match the one on your team page.


6.


**Reclassifying on the return without amending the payroll filings.** Moving a number into officer compensation on Form 1120-S at tax time, with no corresponding W-2 and Forms 941, produces a return that disagrees with the payroll record. The amount is deducted as wages but was never subjected to FICA and never reported to SSA. That fails IRC 3121(d)(1), fails the Notice 2008-1 W-2 condition if health premiums were in the mix, and fails Section 199A(b)(4)(C) for the wage limitation. The correction is a corrected payroll filing, not a return entry.


7.


**Ignoring the loan-versus-distribution and basis questions.** When the owner has been pulling cash informally, two problems arrive together. Glass Blocks Unlimited collapsed the loan-repayment defense by holding that the transfers in were capital contributions rather than bona fide debt, and the IRS guidance on S corporation stock and debt basis is explicit that a loan guarantee alone doesn’t create debt basis. Separately, a non-dividend distribution is tax-free only to the extent of stock basis, and the excess is a capital gain that debt basis won’t shelter. So an owner who took large distributions instead of salary can face reclassified wages and a capital gain in the same year. Form 7203 is where that gets tracked, and the same documentation discipline our[R&D credit questionnaire](https://www.indinero.com/blog/rd-tax-credit-questionnaire/) applies to time records applies here to intercompany cash.


## The R&D Credit + Payroll Connection


Only W-2 wages count as qualified research expenses under IRC 41(b)(2)(A), so a low owner salary shrinks the R&D credit while it saves payroll tax.


You’re not just setting a payroll number. You’re setting the input to three other calculations, and this is the one the competing pages on this phrase leave out entirely.


### Distributions produce no qualified research expense


IRC 41(b)(2)(A) defines in-house research expenses to include any wages paid or incurred to an employee for qualified services, and 41(b)(2)(D) defines wages by cross-reference to Section 3401(a), the income tax withholding definition. Distributions aren’t Section 3401(a) wages.


So an owner who is the company’s principal researcher, taking $20,000 of salary plus $280,000 of distributions, has contributed $20,000 at most to the qualified research expense base. The $280,000 contributes nothing.


That reverses the usual logic in one line. For a company with real research activity, the low owner salary isn’t a pure payroll tax saving. It’s a payroll tax saving financed partly by a smaller credit, and the exchange rate depends on which credit rate the company is on.


### Qualified services and the 80 percent rule


IRC 41(b)(2)(B) defines qualified services as engaging in qualified research, or engaging in the direct supervision or direct support of research activities. The statute then supplies an allocation shortcut. If substantially all of an individual’s services for the year meet that definition, all of that individual’s services count as qualified.


Substantially all is conventionally read as at least 80 percent. For a technical founder, that threshold is the whole ballgame. At 80 percent or more of time on qualified research or its direct supervision or support, 100 percent of that founder’s wages are qualified wages. Below 80 percent, the company allocates, and the allocation needs support that an examiner can follow.


### The documentation an owner allocation needs


Owner wages are the most scrutinized line in an R&D credit study, because the owner controls both the time record and the salary. Four things hold up.


- **Contemporaneous time tracking by business component.** Not a year-end percentage estimate. The credit form is organized by business component, so the records should be too.
- **A written role description** that separates qualified research, direct supervision, and direct support from selling, fundraising, administration, and customer support. Only the first three count.
- **Consistency with the compensation file.** If the reasonable-compensation analysis prices the owner as a CEO running sales and management, and the credit study claims 85 percent of that same owner’s time on qualified research, the two files contradict each other. Examiners read both.
- **Payroll register tie-out.** Qualified wages have to reconcile to the Form W-2 and the Forms 941 actually filed.


### Form 6765 asks about officer wages directly


The IRS built an officer-wage disclosure into the credit form. The[instructions for Form 6765](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i6765) require line 38 to report the total amount of all officer wages included in the qualified wages shown on line 42.


Section G, business component information, is the other current item. It’s optional for tax years beginning before 2026 and required for tax years beginning after 2025. Two exceptions survive for tax year 2026 and later. A qualified small business under Section 41(h)(3) that checks the box to claim the reduced payroll tax credit, and a taxpayer with QREs of $1.5 million or less and average gross receipts of $50 million or less claiming the credit on an original return. The reporting standard is at least 80 percent of total QREs across no more than 50 business components, in descending order by amount.


So for tax year 2026 an owner-operator S corp either elects the payroll offset, stays inside that exception, or starts building business-component detail during the year. That’s a workflow change, and it lands in the same year as everything else on this page.


### The payroll offset is an entity-level mechanic


Here’s the structural asymmetry that makes the owner’s salary decisive, and it’s the part almost nobody models.


The credit passes through. The offset doesn’t. An S corporation files Form 6765 and allocates the research credit to shareholders on Schedule K-1 line 13g, code M, where it lands on the shareholder’s Form 3800. But the payroll tax election under IRC 41(h) is made at the entity level, through Section D of Form 6765. The elected amount then flows to Form 8974 and is claimed on the Form 941 for the quarter that begins after the income tax return is filed, where the first $250,000 can only reduce the employer’s share of Social Security tax, with any remainder applying against Medicare. Unused credit carries forward.


Now the arithmetic for a one-owner company. At a $60,000 owner salary, the entity generates $3,720 of employer OASDI across the whole year. At $160,000, it generates $9,920. A low salary shrinks both sides, the qualified wage base and the pool the credit can actually be monetized against, so the credit sits as a carryforward instead of becoming cash. The quarter-by-quarter mechanics of[applying the R&D credit against payroll taxes](https://www.indinero.com/blog/rd-tax-credit-against-payroll-taxes/) go through that sequencing in detail.


Two eligibility limits travel with the election. A qualified small business needs gross receipts under $5 million for the tax year and no gross receipts for any tax year before the 5-tax-year period ending with the tax year, and the cap is $500,000 for tax years beginning after December 31, 2022. The election can’t be made if it was made for 5 or more preceding tax years, and revoking it takes IRS consent. Members of the same controlled group are treated as a single taxpayer under IRC 41(f)(1), and a shareholder can’t be treated as an eligible small business unless both the S corporation and the shareholder meet the gross receipts test. Owners running two or three related entities need the group run before counting anything.


### Section 174A is current law


Domestic research expensing is back. OBBBA added Section 174A, allowing a deduction for domestic research or experimental expenditures, including domestic software development, paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Section 174A(c) allows an election to capitalize and amortize over not less than 60 months instead. Revenue Procedure 2025-28 supplies the election and method-change procedures, and Notice 2026-07 covers the transition period in which both Section 174 and Section 174A govern timing. Foreign research expenditures stay outside Section 174A and continue under Section 174’s 15-year amortization.


Any guide still describing mandatory five-year domestic amortization as current law is out of date, which matters here because the deduction and the credit interact. The Section 280C reduced credit election, made at Item A on an original timely filed return and irrevocable once made, drops the regular rate from 20 percent to 15.8 percent. Skip that election and you reduce your Section 174A expenditures by the amount of the credit instead. Our breakdown of[Section 174 capitalization](https://www.indinero.com/blog/section-174-rd-capitalization-explained-2026/) covers how that choice plays out across a full return.

It’s that the number has four moving parts and has to be computed.

## Frequently asked questions


These come up on almost every owner-compensation engagement, usually right after the first year the company has real profit to distribute. Here are the questions we answer most often.


### How much salary is reasonable for an S-corp owner?


Reasonable compensation for an S-corp owner is whatever comparable employers pay for the services that shareholder-employee actually performs, documented with wage survey data. There’s no safe harbor and no statutory percentage. Build the number from what the owner does, priced against Bureau of Labor Statistics wage data for the right SOC code and geography. Vendor salary tables aren’t survey data. Indinero builds that comparability file before the first payroll run, then keeps it consistent with the W-2 and the Form 1120-S.


### Can an S-corp owner take distributions without running any payroll?


An S-corp owner who performs more than minor services can’t take distributions without payroll, because a working corporate officer is a statutory employee. The only exception covers an officer who performs no or minor services and neither receives nor is entitled to receive remuneration. Both halves have to be true. Routing the money as a 1099 fee or a loan repayment doesn’t help either. Courts recharacterized both arrangements as wages in Joseph M. Grey Public Accountant and Glass Blocks Unlimited.


### What happens when the IRS reclassifies distributions as wages?


Reclassified distributions become wages subject to FICA, FUTA, and income tax withholding, with interest and penalties, under Rev. Rul. 74-44. The corporation owes the employment tax, failure-to-deposit penalties, and penalties for the missing Form W-2, and a responsible person can be personally liable for the trust-fund portion. Reclassifying on the Form 1120-S at tax time without amending the payroll filings doesn’t fix it. That amount never carried FICA and never reached the Social Security Administration. The fix is a corrected payroll filing.


### Is the 60/40 split between salary and distributions an actual IRS rule?


The 60/40 split between salary and distributions isn’t an IRS rule, and neither is the one-third rule or any other fixed ratio. There’s no safe harbor and no statutory percentage anywhere in the Code or the case law. The IRS lists the use of a formula as one of nine factors, so a ratio describes your process without defending your number. Comparable pay for comparable services is the standard, which is why indinero prices the owner’s actual duties against wage survey data.


### How does the owner’s salary affect the Section 199A deduction?


The owner’s salary moves the Section 199A deduction in two directions, and which one wins depends on taxable income and SSTB status. Owner wages aren’t qualified business income, so they shrink the 20 percent base. They also feed the 199A(b)(2) wage limitation at 50 percent of W-2 wages, so above the threshold a higher salary can raise the deduction. Below the threshold the limitation never applies and the effect reverses. An SSTB above the phase-in top gets no deduction at any salary.


### Can owner wages count toward the R&D tax credit?


Owner wages do count toward the R&D credit, but only W-2 wages become qualified research expenses under IRC 41(b)(2), so distributions produce nothing. A low owner salary shrinks the qualified wage base, which is the trap for a founder doing the research. Form 6765 line 38 requires reporting officer wages included in qualified wages. The credit passes through on Schedule K-1, but the Form 8974 payroll offset lands against employer Social Security tax at the entity, which a low salary also shrinks.


### When in the year do an owner’s W-2 wages have to be run?


Owner W-2 wages should be run on a regular payroll schedule during the year, not as a single December catch-up. Section 199A(b)(4)(C) disqualifies W-2 wages from the wage limitation unless the amount is properly included in a return filed with the Social Security Administration within 60 days of its due date. A year-end scramble producing a late or corrected W-2 can forfeit that limitation. A monthly or semimonthly owner payroll, which is how indinero runs it, keeps deposits inside the normal schedule.
